name: Scalp exfoliation

image.caption: New and Seanik shampoo bars, Ocean Salt face scrub, Dream Cream, Roots scalp treatment - Lush Handmade Cosmetics

lead: Scalp exfoliation uses physical scrubs, chemical exfoliants such as salicylic or glycolic acid, or hybrids to remove dead skin cells, oil and product buildup from the scalp. People use it for fewer visible flakes and a cleaner look, and some say it helps products absorb and supports hair growth.

Physical granules rub debris off, and acids loosen bonds between dead skin cells. Salicylic acid is an FDA-approved over-the-counter anti-dandruff active, and a 2024 study evaluated a hydroxy acid scrub with a copper tripeptide serum in adults with seborrheic dermatitis. No studies were found testing scalp exfoliation for hair growth.

paras: People massage a scrub or acid treatment into the scalp before or during shampooing, then rinse, typically once a week or less. It is often combined with dandruff shampoos or scalp serums. Reduced flaking is visible after a few uses.
Overdoing it may cause dryness, oiliness or irritation. People with psoriasis, eczema or open sores are advised to consult a dermatologist first.

angle.text: Scalp exfoliation clears flakes and product buildup, so your scalp and hair look cleaner, and some users say it also supports growth. Salicylic acid is an approved dandruff active, but no studies have tested exfoliation for hair growth.

lead: Scalp exfoliation is a hair-care practice that uses physical scrubs, chemical exfoliants such as salicylic or glycolic acid, or hybrids to remove dead skin cells, oil and product buildup from the scalp.[1] People use it to reduce visible flakes, leave hair looking cleaner and fuller at the roots, and keep a clear scalp as a base for hair-care products, which they say supports healthy-looking hair and hair growth.[1][2]

Salicylic acid is an FDA-approved over-the-counter anti-dandruff active, and dandruff shampoos combine actives such as zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole.[3] Wikipedia's article on cosmetic exfoliation describes chemical exfoliants as acids and enzymes that loosen bonds between dead skin cells, with beta-hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid acting within pores, and notes dermatologists say exfoliation is not medically necessary because skin sheds naturally.[4]
One 2024 study evaluated a hydroxy acid scrub combined with a copper tripeptide serum in adults with seborrheic dermatitis.[5] No studies were found testing scalp exfoliation for hair growth.
infobox: Salt, sugar, charcoal; salicylic, glycolic, lactic acids[1]
Less flaking, clearer follicles, better product absorption[1]

paras: Physical exfoliants use granules such as sugar, sea salt or charcoal, rubbed in with massage. Chemical exfoliants use acids that dissolve bonds between dead skin cells.[1]

Wikipedia notes that chemical exfoliation is often suggested for acne and that overdoing exfoliation can damage the skin barrier, causing tightness, sensitivity, redness and dryness.[4] On T Nation, a poster advised massaging shampoo in gently with the fingertips instead of rough scrubbing, and another suggested scalp massage may support blood flow.[6] A TRT-focused poster described gently scrubbing the scalp with fingers on days he used ketoconazole, saying he had read that sebum buildup could accelerate hair loss.[7]

Descriptions claim exfoliation unclogs follicles and supports hair growth.[1] Dermatology references on dandruff describe cause as involving sebum, Malassezia yeasts and individual sensitivity, and list antifungal and keratolytic shampoos as treatments.[3]
Descriptions say over-exfoliation may disrupt the scalp barrier, causing dryness, extra oil or discomfort, and suggest people with psoriasis, eczema or open sores consult a dermatologist.[1]

A 2024 study in Cureus assessed the safety, efficacy and tolerability of a regimen combining a hydroxy acid scrub with a copper tripeptide serum for seborrheic dermatitis in adults.[5] No studies were found on exfoliation alone for hair growth or density.

lore.intro: On T Nation, scalp scrubbing comes up in hair-loss and dandruff threads, usually as gentle washing or fingertip scrubbing alongside medicated shampoo.[6][7]
